title: Night, Weather & Hazards
summary: How to see and be seen at night, handle rain, fog, snow, ice, wind and floods, and spot hazards like animals, debris and work zones early.

blocks.text: Night driving is more dangerous because you cannot see as far ahead or as well to the sides. It is also harder to judge distances and see colors. Pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists are much harder to see, especially in dark clothing.

items: Turn on your headlights as soon as daylight begins to fade, so others can see you. Your state also sets a legal time for headlight use; check your State Cheat Sheet.
Daytime running lights are not enough at dusk. They usually do not turn on your taillights. Use your headlights.
Clean your windshield and headlights before a night drive. Dirt adds glare and cuts the light your headlights give.
After leaving a brightly lit place, such as a gas station, drive slowly until your eyes adjust to the dark.
Dawn and dusk are risky: light is poor and deer and other animals are most active.
Never overdrive your headlights. Drive slowly enough to stop within the distance they light up.

rows: Best on dark, open roads with no one nearby. Do not use them in fog, rain or snow; the light reflects back at you.
Use when a vehicle comes toward you, when you follow another vehicle, and in rain, snow or fog, even in daytime.

blocks.text: How close you can be to an oncoming or leading vehicle before you must dim your high beams varies by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet.

items: If oncoming headlights blind you, look toward the right edge of the road and watch the other car out of the corner of your eye.
If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, do not switch yours on to get back at them; that only blinds you both. Stay on low beams and look toward the right edge until they pass.
If lights behind you glare in your inside mirror, flip the mirror to its night setting.
A single oncoming headlight could be a motorcycle, a bicycle or a car with one light out. Keep to the right.
For low sun glare, use your sun visor and sunglasses, and keep the windshield clean.
When the sun is low behind you, oncoming drivers are looking into it and may not see you or your signals.

blocks.text: Roads are most slippery in the first few minutes of a rain, when water mixes with oil and grime on the pavement. Slow down and add following distance.

Hydroplaning happens when water builds up under your tires faster than they can push it away, so the tires ride on water instead of the road. A sloshing sound from your tires means there is enough water to risk it.

items: Prevent it: slow down, steer around standing water when you safely can, and keep good tread and proper tire pressure.
If you hydroplane: ease off the gas and hold the wheel steady. Avoid hard braking and sudden steering.
Do not use cruise control on wet, icy or snowy roads. It can keep feeding power if the wheels slip.
In a downpour where you can barely see, slow down. If you still cannot see, pull fully off the road.
If the inside of your windows fogs up, use the defroster or open a window slightly.
After driving through deep water, test your brakes. If they feel weak or pull, drive slowly and brake lightly until they dry.

blocks.text: Turn Around, Don't Drown. Never drive into a flooded road, even if it looks shallow. About 6 inches of water reaches the bottom of most cars and can cause stalling or loss of control. About 2 feet of moving water can carry away most SUVs and pickups. The water can hide a washed-out road. If your car stalls in rising water, get out quickly and move to higher ground.

items: Use low beams. Never drive in fog with only parking lights on.
Use the right edge line as a guide to stay in your lane.
Check your speedometer often. Without visual clues it is easy to creep faster than you realize.
Drive slowly enough to stop within the distance you can see.
Increase your following distance and avoid changing lanes or passing.

blocks.text: If the fog becomes too thick to drive safely, pull completely off the road, preferably into a parking area, turn on your flashers and wait. Do not stop in a travel lane.

items: Bridges and overpasses freeze first, and shady spots under trees or buildings stay icy after the rest of the road is clear.
Black ice is a thin, clear layer of ice that makes the road look wet. If the road looks wet on a freezing day but cars ahead throw no spray, suspect ice: ease off and avoid sudden moves.
Ice is most slippery near the freezing point, when it is wet on top.
Wet leaves can be as slick as ice.
Brake, steer and accelerate gently and smoothly. Skids are usually caused by too much speed plus sudden moves.
Start braking for stops much earlier and more gently than usual.
Slow down on the straight road before a curve. Braking hard in an icy curve can start a skid.
Four-wheel or all-wheel drive helps you get moving, but it does not help you stop any sooner or keep you from skidding.
On a snowy hill, hang back from the car ahead so you won't have to stop partway up.

Stay well back from a working snowplow. The driver sees little behind, may stop or turn around, and throws salt and snow. Its side blades can stick out several feet, so the safest choice is not to pass it.

blocks.text: Before you drive, clear all windows, mirrors and lights, plus the roof and hood. Snow left on top can slide onto your windshield or blow onto drivers behind you.

For winter trips, carry a blanket, warm clothes, a shovel, sand, food and a flashlight. If you get stranded in a storm, stay in your car; it gives shelter and is easier for rescuers to find. Run the engine only briefly for heat and keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow.

items: In strong winds, slow down and keep a firm grip on the wheel.
Expect a sudden crosswind when you leave a sheltered stretch for an open area like a bridge.
Campers, trucks and vehicles pulling trailers are most affected by crosswinds.
On gravel or dirt, slow down. You need more room to stop and can skid more easily.
Slow down on roads with many potholes. They can jolt the car and make the tires lose grip.

Look well ahead for debris so you can avoid it smoothly. If a small object, like a piece of tire tread, appears suddenly with traffic beside you, a sudden swerve can cause a worse crash; slow down and drive over it instead.

blocks.text: Before a long, steep downhill, shift into a lower gear so the engine helps hold your speed. Do not ride your brakes all the way down; constant braking can overheat them so they fade. Never coast in neutral, which removes engine braking.
Runaway truck ramps are only for vehicles that cannot stop. Never stop or park on one.

items: Expect sudden stops, shifting lanes, and workers and equipment close to traffic.
Slow down and leave extra following distance.
If cones and arrow panels show your lane is closed ahead, slow down and merge into the open lane when it is safe.
Obey work-zone signs until you pass the end of the zone, even at night when you see no workers.

blocks.caption: Fines for work-zone violations may be higher. Rules vary by state; check your State Cheat Sheet.

items: Keep your eyes moving: look far ahead and to the sides of the road.
Check your mirrors regularly, even when you are not changing lanes.
Expect others to make mistakes. A car approaching a STOP sign on a side road might not stop, so be ready.
When hazards on both sides are about equal, like parked cars on one side and oncoming traffic on the other, slow down and steer a middle path. If one is more dangerous, give it more room.

blocks.text: Deer and other animals are most active at dawn and dusk. At night, scan the road edges for eyes shining in your headlights. Deer travel in groups, so if one crosses, slow down and expect more.

blocks.caption: At dusk, watch the road edges. Where there is one deer, there are often more.

blocks.text: If an animal runs in front of you, brake firmly and stay in your lane. Do not swerve: swerving can cause a far worse crash with another vehicle, a tree or a pole.

keyPoints: Turn on headlights early, use low beams near other vehicles and in rain, fog or snow, and look to the right edge when blinded.
Roads are slickest when rain first starts; if you hydroplane, ease off the gas and hold the wheel steady.
Never drive into floodwater: 6 inches can stall a car and 2 feet of moving water can float most SUVs.
In fog, use low beams, follow the right edge line, and pull fully off the road if you can't see.
Bridges, overpasses and shady spots freeze first; black ice looks like a wet road.
On snow and ice, do everything gently and early; four-wheel drive does not help you stop.
Use a lower gear on steep downhills instead of riding the brakes.
Scan far ahead and to the sides, and watch for animals at dawn and dusk.
